_link.title: I can describe the cause and consequences of type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes and Graves' disease

options.text: Immune cells attack and destroy the beta cells of the pancreas
options.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the islets of Langerhans.

options.text: Long-term insulin resistance from poor diet and inactivity
options.explanation: Long-term insulin resistance describes type 2 diabetes. Type 1 is caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells.

options.text: Antibodies bind to TSH receptors and overstimulate the thyroid
options.explanation: This describes Graves' disease, not type 1 diabetes.

options.text: Excessive sugar intake damages the pancreas directly
options.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition, not caused by dietary sugar intake damaging the pancreas.

toLevel2.stem: Which type of diabetes accounts for approximately 90% of all cases?

options.text: Type 2 diabetes
options.explanation: Type 2 diabetes represents approximately 90% of all diabetes cases. Type 1 represents about 10%.

options.text: Type 1 diabetes
options.explanation: Type 1 diabetes represents approximately 10% of all diabetes cases, not 90%.

options.text: Graves' disease
options.explanation: Graves' disease is a thyroid condition, not a type of diabetes.

options.text: Both types equally
options.explanation: The types are not equally prevalent. Type 2 accounts for about 90% and type 1 about 10%.

toLevel2.stem: In Graves' disease, what do the abnormal antibodies do?

options.text: They mimic TSH and bind to TSH receptors on the thyroid, overstimulating thyroxine production
options.explanation: In Graves' disease, the immune system produces antibodies that bind to TSH receptors on the thyroid, causing continuous overproduction of thyroxine (hyperthyroidism).

options.text: They destroy beta cells in the pancreas
options.explanation: Destruction of beta cells describes type 1 diabetes, not Graves' disease.

options.text: They block insulin receptors on liver cells
options.explanation: Blocking insulin receptors relates to insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes, not Graves' disease.

options.text: They attack the hypothalamus and prevent hormone release
options.explanation: In Graves' disease, antibodies target TSH receptors on the thyroid, not the hypothalamus.

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following is a common symptom of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Excessive thirst and increased urination
options.explanation: Both types of diabetes cause hyperglycaemia, which leads to excessive thirst, increased urination, tiredness, lethargy, weight gain, dizziness and constant hunger.

options.text: Weight loss and increased heart rate
options.explanation: Weight loss and increased heart rate are symptoms of Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism), not typical diabetes symptoms.

options.text: Enlarged thyroid gland and hair loss
options.explanation: Enlarged thyroid and hair loss are symptoms of Graves' disease, not diabetes.

options.text: Cold intolerance and fatigue
options.explanation: Cold intolerance is a symptom of hypothyroidism. While fatigue can occur in diabetes, the combination with cold intolerance points to thyroid disorder.

toLevel2.stem: What condition does Graves' disease cause?

options.text: Hyperthyroidism — overproduction of thyroxine
options.explanation: Graves' disease causes hyperthyroidism because antibodies continuously stimulate the thyroid to overproduce thyroxine, increasing metabolic rate above normal.

options.text: Hypothyroidism — underproduction of thyroxine
options.explanation: Graves' disease causes overproduction of thyroxine (hyperthyroidism), not underproduction (hypothyroidism).

options.text: Hyperglycaemia — elevated blood glucose
options.explanation: Hyperglycaemia is associated with diabetes, not Graves' disease. Graves' affects the thyroid and thyroxine production.

options.text: Hypocalcaemia — low blood calcium
options.explanation: Hypocalcaemia relates to parathyroid or calcitonin disorders. Graves' disease specifically involves excess thyroxine production.

toLevel2.stem: Type 2 diabetes is caused by long-term insulin resistance, often linked to obesity and reduced physical activity.
toLevel2.explanation: Type 2 diabetes results from insulin resistance over a long period, with changes in diet and reduced physical activity being the main contributing factors. It represents approximately 90% of diabetes cases.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. Type 2 diabetes is indeed caused by insulin resistance, linked to lifestyle factors including obesity and inactivity.

toLevel2.stem: Type 1 diabetes can be prevented through diet and exercise.
toLevel2.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease that cannot be cured or prevented. It occurs when immune cells destroy beta cells. Diet and exercise can help manage type 2 diabetes.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is false. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and cannot be prevented. Diet and exercise management relates to type 2 diabetes.

toLevel2.stem: In type 1 diabetes, {{blank:1}} cells are destroyed by the immune system, eliminating the production of {{blank:2}}.
Graves' disease causes {{blank:1}} because antibodies overstimulate the thyroid to produce excess {{blank:2}}.
In type 2 diabetes, {{blank:1}} resistance causes beta cells to overproduce and eventually become {{blank:2}}.

toLevel3.stem: How does the cause of type 1 diabetes differ from the cause of type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Type 1 involves autoimmune destruction of beta cells, while type 2 involves gradual insulin resistance that exhausts beta cells
options.explanation: In type 1, the immune system attacks and destroys beta cells directly. In type 2, cells become resistant to insulin over time, forcing beta cells to overproduce until they can no longer keep up.

options.text: Type 1 is caused by overeating and type 2 is caused by the immune system
options.explanation: This is reversed. Type 1 is autoimmune (not caused by diet), while type 2 is associated with lifestyle factors including obesity.

options.text: Type 1 affects the thyroid and type 2 affects the pancreas
options.explanation: Both types of diabetes affect the pancreas. It is Graves' disease that affects the thyroid.

options.text: There is no meaningful difference; both types have the same cause
options.explanation: The causes are fundamentally different: autoimmune beta cell destruction (type 1) versus insulin resistance and beta cell exhaustion (type 2).

toLevel3.stem: Why does hyperglycaemia occur in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes despite having different causes?

options.text: In both types, insulin cannot effectively lower blood glucose — either because it is absent (type 1) or because cells are resistant to it (type 2)
options.explanation: Both conditions result in glucose remaining in the blood. In type 1, no insulin is produced. In type 2, insulin is produced but target cells do not respond effectively. Either way, glucose is not absorbed by cells.

options.text: Both types produce too much glucagon, which raises blood glucose
options.explanation: Excess glucagon is not the primary issue in either type. The problem is that insulin cannot effectively promote glucose uptake by cells.

options.text: In both types, the liver releases too much stored glucose
options.explanation: While unregulated glucagon can cause some liver glucose release, the primary issue is that insulin cannot drive glucose into cells, leaving blood glucose elevated.

options.text: Both types cause the pancreas to produce excess glucose directly
options.explanation: The pancreas produces hormones, not glucose. Hyperglycaemia results from insulin being absent or ineffective at promoting glucose uptake by target cells.

toLevel3.stem: Why does Graves' disease cause weight loss rather than weight gain?

options.text: Excess thyroxine increases metabolic rate, causing the body to burn more energy than normal
options.explanation: Thyroxine increases metabolic rate in all tissues. In Graves' disease, excess thyroxine drives metabolism far above normal, causing rapid energy expenditure and weight loss despite increased appetite.

options.text: The antibodies destroy fat cells directly
options.explanation: The antibodies in Graves' disease target TSH receptors on the thyroid, not fat cells. Weight loss results from increased metabolic rate due to excess thyroxine.

options.text: Graves' disease prevents nutrient absorption in the intestines
options.explanation: Graves' disease affects the thyroid, not the digestive system. Weight loss is due to increased metabolism from excess thyroxine, not malabsorption.

options.text: The thyroid gland absorbs nutrients that would normally go to body tissues
options.explanation: The enlarged thyroid in Graves' disease does not absorb significant nutrients. Weight loss is caused by the body-wide increase in metabolic rate from excess thyroxine.

toLevel3.stem: Why do type 1 diabetes sufferers require daily insulin injections while type 2 sufferers may initially manage with diet and exercise?

options.text: In type 1, beta cells are completely destroyed so no insulin is produced; in type 2, some beta cells still function and can be supported by lifestyle changes
options.explanation: Type 1 patients have no insulin production at all, making injections essential. Type 2 patients still produce some insulin initially, and reducing insulin resistance through diet and exercise can improve glucose control.

options.text: Type 1 is more severe than type 2 in all cases
options.explanation: Severity varies. The key difference is that type 1 has zero insulin production (absolute deficiency), while type 2 has reduced effectiveness (relative deficiency) that can initially be managed.

options.text: Type 2 is not a real disease and does not need treatment
options.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is a serious condition. While initially manageable with lifestyle changes, most sufferers eventually require medication or insulin injections.

options.text: Insulin injections only work for autoimmune conditions
options.explanation: Insulin injections work in both types. Type 1 requires them from diagnosis because no insulin is produced. Most type 2 sufferers eventually need them too as beta cells become exhausted.

toLevel3.stem: Explain why both type 1 diabetes and Graves' disease are classified as autoimmune conditions.

options.text: Both involve the immune system attacking the body's own cells or receptors: type 1 destroys beta cells, and Graves' produces antibodies that stimulate thyroid receptors
options.explanation: In autoimmune conditions, the immune system malfunctions and targets the body's own tissues. In type 1, immune cells destroy beta cells. In Graves', antibodies bind to TSH receptors as if they were TSH.

options.text: Both are caused by bacterial infections that trigger immune responses
options.explanation: Neither condition is caused by bacterial infection. Both are autoimmune — the immune system attacks the body's own tissues without an external pathogen.

options.text: Both conditions result in the immune system being too weak to function
options.explanation: Autoimmune diseases involve an overactive or misdirected immune response, not a weak one. The immune system attacks the body's own tissues.

options.text: Both are classified as autoimmune because they can be cured by antibiotics
options.explanation: Autoimmune diseases cannot be cured by antibiotics. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections. Neither type 1 diabetes nor Graves' disease currently has a cure.

toLevel3.stem: What happens to beta cells in the progression of type 2 diabetes?

options.text: They overproduce insulin to compensate for resistance, and over time become exhausted and unable to produce enough
options.explanation: As target cells become insulin resistant, beta cells increase insulin output. This prolonged overproduction eventually exhausts the beta cells, reducing insulin output and worsening blood glucose control.

options.text: They are immediately destroyed by the immune system
options.explanation: Immediate immune destruction of beta cells describes type 1 diabetes, not type 2. In type 2, beta cells gradually become exhausted from overwork.

options.text: They stop producing insulin immediately when resistance develops
options.explanation: Beta cell decline in type 2 is gradual, not immediate. They first overproduce to compensate, then slowly become exhausted over years.

options.text: They multiply rapidly to meet the increased demand for insulin
options.explanation: Beta cells cannot multiply sufficiently to meet demand. They overproduce from existing cells and eventually become exhausted.

toLevel3.stem: In Graves' disease, the normal negative feedback mechanism successfully controls thyroxine production.
toLevel3.explanation: In Graves' disease, negative feedback reduces TSH from the pituitary, but the antibodies continue stimulating the thyroid independently of this feedback loop. The thyroid remains overstimulated because the antibodies are not regulated by the feedback mechanism.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is false. Negative feedback does suppress TSH, but the antibodies bypass this control and continue stimulating the thyroid independently.

toLevel3.stem: Type 1 diabetes involves {{blank:1}} destruction of beta cells, while type 2 involves gradual {{blank:2}} of beta cells from overwork.
Graves' disease causes weight loss because excess {{blank:1}} increases {{blank:2}} far above normal levels.
In Graves' disease, antibodies bypass the normal {{blank:1}} loop by binding directly to {{blank:2}} receptors on the thyroid.

toLevel4.stem: A patient has high blood glucose and low insulin levels. Which condition is most consistent with these results?

options.text: Type 1 diabetes, because destroyed beta cells cannot produce insulin
options.explanation: Low insulin with high glucose indicates that beta cells are not producing insulin. This is characteristic of type 1 diabetes, where autoimmune destruction eliminates insulin production.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes, because insulin resistance always means low insulin
options.explanation: In early type 2 diabetes, insulin levels are often high (beta cells overproduce to compensate). Low insulin occurs only in later stages when beta cells become exhausted.

options.text: Graves' disease, because excess thyroxine destroys insulin
options.explanation: Graves' disease affects the thyroid and thyroxine, not insulin production in the pancreas.

options.text: Hypothyroidism, because low thyroxine reduces insulin secretion
options.explanation: Hypothyroidism involves the thyroid, not the pancreas. The combination of high glucose and low insulin points to a pancreatic disorder like type 1 diabetes.

toLevel4.stem: A patient has high blood glucose and high insulin levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Type 2 diabetes, because beta cells are overproducing insulin to overcome target cell resistance
options.explanation: High insulin with high glucose indicates that insulin is being produced but target cells are not responding. This is characteristic of the insulin resistance seen in type 2 diabetes.

options.text: Type 1 diabetes, because the immune system has not yet fully destroyed beta cells
options.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is characterised by low or absent insulin due to beta cell destruction. High insulin levels are inconsistent with type 1.

options.text: Graves' disease, because excess thyroxine stimulates insulin production
options.explanation: Graves' disease involves thyroid overactivation, not direct effects on insulin production.

options.text: Normal physiology after a large meal
options.explanation: After a meal, insulin rises but successfully lowers blood glucose. Persistently high glucose despite high insulin indicates insulin resistance.

toLevel4.stem: A Graves' disease patient is treated with radioiodine therapy. Explain how this treatment works.

options.text: Radioactive iodine is taken up by overactive thyroid cells and kills them, reducing thyroxine production
options.explanation: Thyroid cells naturally absorb iodine for thyroxine production. Radioactive iodine is selectively taken up by these cells, where it destroys the overactive tissue and reduces excess thyroxine output.

options.text: Radioactive iodine destroys the TSH-mimicking antibodies in the blood
options.explanation: Radioiodine targets thyroid cells that absorb iodine, not circulating antibodies. The treatment reduces thyroid tissue, not the antibodies causing the disease.

options.text: Radioactive iodine stimulates the immune system to stop producing antibodies
options.explanation: Radioiodine does not affect the immune system. It specifically targets iodine-absorbing thyroid cells to reduce the gland's ability to produce excess thyroxine.

options.text: Radioactive iodine blocks TSH receptors on the thyroid permanently
options.explanation: Radioiodine does not block receptors. It kills overactive thyroid cells that absorb it, physically reducing the amount of thyroid tissue available to produce thyroxine.

toLevel4.stem: A person with type 2 diabetes begins a regular exercise programme and improves their diet. Why might this help manage their blood glucose levels?

options.text: Exercise and diet improvements can reduce insulin resistance, allowing existing insulin to be more effective at promoting glucose uptake
options.explanation: Physical activity increases cell sensitivity to insulin, meaning the insulin produced by beta cells works more effectively. Dietary changes reduce the glucose load. Together, they can improve blood glucose control without additional medication.

options.text: Exercise causes beta cells to regenerate and produce more insulin
options.explanation: Exercise does not regenerate destroyed or exhausted beta cells. It works by improving the sensitivity of target cells to the insulin that is already being produced.

options.text: Diet changes cure the autoimmune response that caused type 2 diabetes
options.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is not autoimmune (that is type 1). Diet changes help manage type 2 by reducing glucose intake and improving insulin sensitivity, not by curing an autoimmune response.

options.text: Exercise directly lowers blood glucose by breaking down glucose in muscle tissue, independent of insulin
options.explanation: While muscles do use glucose during exercise, the primary long-term benefit is improved insulin sensitivity. Exercise helps insulin work more effectively, which is the key management strategy.

toLevel4.stem: A patient presents with weight loss, increased heart rate, warm skin and an enlarged thyroid gland. Which condition do these symptoms suggest?

options.text: Graves' disease, because these are symptoms of hyperthyroidism caused by excess thyroxine
options.explanation: Weight loss (high metabolism), increased heart rate, warm skin (excess heat production) and enlarged thyroid (overstimulation) are classic Graves' disease symptoms resulting from excess thyroxine production.

options.text: Type 1 diabetes, because beta cells have been destroyed
options.explanation: Type 1 diabetes symptoms include excessive thirst, increased urination and tiredness. Weight loss can occur in diabetes, but the other symptoms described are specific to hyperthyroidism.

options.text: Hypothyroidism, because the thyroid is not producing enough thyroxine
options.explanation: Hypothyroidism causes weight gain, fatigue and cold intolerance — opposite to the symptoms described. These symptoms indicate hyperthyroidism.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes, because of insulin resistance
options.explanation: Type 2 diabetes symptoms include thirst, urination changes and fatigue. The described symptoms (weight loss, high heart rate, warm skin, enlarged thyroid) point to Graves' disease.

toLevel4.stem: Why do most type 2 diabetes sufferers eventually require insulin injections despite initially managing with diet and exercise?

options.text: Because beta cells become progressively exhausted from long-term overproduction and can no longer produce sufficient insulin
options.explanation: In type 2 diabetes, beta cells compensate for resistance by overproducing insulin. Over years, this exhausts the cells and insulin output drops, eventually requiring external insulin.

options.text: Because the immune system eventually destroys the beta cells, converting type 2 into type 1
options.explanation: Type 2 does not convert to type 1. Beta cell exhaustion in type 2 is from overwork, not immune destruction. The underlying mechanisms remain different.

options.text: Because exercise becomes ineffective after age 50
options.explanation: Exercise remains beneficial at any age. The need for insulin arises because beta cells become progressively exhausted, not because exercise stops working.

options.text: Because insulin injections are cheaper than maintaining a healthy diet
options.explanation: The transition to insulin injections is driven by the medical progression of beta cell exhaustion, not by cost considerations.

toLevel4.stem: Predict the TSH levels in a patient with untreated Graves' disease. Explain your reasoning.

options.text: TSH levels would be low because excess thyroxine triggers negative feedback that suppresses TSH release from the pituitary
options.explanation: High thyroxine from the overstimulated thyroid feeds back to inhibit TRH and TSH. The pituitary responds normally to the elevated thyroxine by reducing TSH, even though the thyroid is still stimulated by antibodies.

options.text: TSH levels would be high because the thyroid is overactive
options.explanation: An overactive thyroid produces excess thyroxine, which triggers negative feedback and suppresses TSH. TSH levels would be low, not high.

options.text: TSH levels would be normal because the feedback system compensates perfectly
options.explanation: The feedback system reduces TSH in response to high thyroxine, but cannot resolve the underlying issue of antibody stimulation. TSH drops below normal.

options.text: TSH levels would fluctuate randomly because the disease disrupts all regulation
options.explanation: The negative feedback system still functions predictably. High thyroxine consistently suppresses TSH. The dysfunction is the antibodies bypassing this regulation at the thyroid level.

toLevel4.stem: High blood glucose with {{blank:1}} insulin levels suggests type 1 diabetes, while high glucose with {{blank:2}} insulin levels suggests type 2.
Radioiodine therapy works because thyroid cells selectively {{blank:1}} iodine, and the radioactive form {{blank:2}} the overactive cells.
In untreated Graves' disease, TSH levels are {{blank:1}} because excess thyroxine triggers {{blank:2}} on the pituitary.

toLevel5.stem: Compare the mechanisms by which type 1 diabetes and Graves' disease disrupt normal endocrine function, identifying which step of the hormone process is affected in each.

options.text: Type 1 disrupts step 1 (hormone secretion) by destroying the cells that produce insulin; Graves' disrupts step 3 (receptor binding) by having antibodies bind in place of TSH
options.explanation: In type 1, the source of insulin is eliminated (step 1 failure). In Graves', the thyroid's TSH receptors are bound by antibodies instead of TSH (step 3 hijacking). Both are autoimmune but affect different steps.

options.text: Both diseases disrupt step 1 because both involve destruction of endocrine cells
options.explanation: Graves' disease does not destroy endocrine cells — it overstimulates them via antibodies binding to receptors. Only type 1 involves cell destruction.

options.text: Type 1 disrupts step 3 and Graves' disrupts step 1
options.explanation: This is reversed. Type 1 eliminates insulin-producing cells (step 1), while Graves' involves receptor binding by antibodies (step 3).

options.text: Both diseases disrupt step 2 because hormones cannot travel in the blood
options.explanation: Neither disease affects blood transport of hormones. Type 1 affects hormone production and Graves' affects receptor binding.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that type 2 diabetes is entirely the patient's fault because it is linked to lifestyle factors. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: The claim is an oversimplification; while lifestyle factors contribute significantly, genetic predisposition, socioeconomic factors and the food environment also play important roles
options.explanation: Type 2 diabetes has clear lifestyle links (diet, exercise), but genetic susceptibility, access to healthy food, and environmental factors all contribute. Blaming individuals ignores the complex interplay of risk factors.

options.text: The claim is completely correct because only diet and exercise cause type 2 diabetes
options.explanation: While diet and exercise are major contributing factors, genetic predisposition and environmental factors also play significant roles. The condition is multifactorial.

options.text: The claim is completely wrong because type 2 diabetes is entirely genetic
options.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is not entirely genetic. Lifestyle factors including diet and physical activity are major contributing factors, along with genetic and environmental components.

options.text: The claim is correct because type 2 diabetes can always be cured by exercise
options.explanation: Type 2 diabetes cannot always be cured by exercise. While lifestyle changes help manage it, most sufferers eventually require medication. The disease involves progressive beta cell exhaustion.

toLevel5.stem: Why is Graves' disease particularly difficult to treat compared to hypothyroidism?

options.text: Because the root cause (autoimmune antibody production) cannot be stopped, whereas hypothyroidism can be managed by simply replacing the missing thyroxine
options.explanation: Hypothyroidism treatment is straightforward: replace thyroxine with tablets. Graves' disease requires targeting the immune system or destroying/removing thyroid tissue because the antibodies continuously stimulate the thyroid regardless of feedback.

options.text: Because Graves' disease has more symptoms than hypothyroidism
options.explanation: The number of symptoms does not determine treatment difficulty. The fundamental challenge is that the autoimmune cause of Graves' disease cannot be directly stopped.

options.text: Because hypothyroidism is always fatal and Graves' disease is not
options.explanation: Neither condition is typically fatal with treatment. The difficulty difference lies in targeting the root cause, not in mortality.

options.text: Because there are no medications available for Graves' disease
options.explanation: There are treatments (anti-thyroid drugs, radioiodine, surgery), but they target the thyroid rather than the immune cause. Hypothyroidism is simpler because hormone replacement directly addresses the deficiency.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the three treatment options for Graves' disease (anti-thyroid drugs, radioiodine therapy and surgery) in terms of their approach to the underlying problem.

options.text: All three target the thyroid's ability to produce thyroxine rather than the immune cause; they manage symptoms but do not cure the autoimmune dysfunction
options.explanation: Anti-thyroid drugs block thyroxine synthesis. Radioiodine kills thyroid cells. Surgery removes thyroid tissue. None addresses the antibodies causing the overstimulation. All are effective management strategies but not cures.

options.text: All three directly stop antibody production and cure the autoimmune cause
options.explanation: None of the treatments stop antibody production. They all target the thyroid to reduce thyroxine output while the antibodies continue to be produced.

options.text: Only surgery cures the disease while drugs and radioiodine are temporary
options.explanation: Even surgery does not cure the autoimmune cause — the antibodies persist. Surgery removes the thyroid tissue they act on, preventing thyroxine overproduction but potentially causing hypothyroidism.

options.text: Anti-thyroid drugs are the only effective treatment; the other two are outdated
options.explanation: All three treatments remain in use and are effective. The choice depends on severity, patient factors and preferences. Each has advantages and limitations.

toLevel5.stem: A patient who has had Graves' disease treated with thyroid removal surgery now requires daily thyroxine tablets. Analyse why this is necessary.

options.text: Removing the thyroid eliminates the source of thyroxine, creating hypothyroidism that must be managed with hormone replacement
options.explanation: Surgery solved the hyperthyroidism by removing the overactive thyroid. However, without the thyroid, the body cannot produce any thyroxine, so the patient now has the opposite problem and needs external thyroxine to maintain metabolic function.

options.text: The thyroxine tablets prevent the antibodies from attacking other glands
options.explanation: Thyroxine tablets replace the hormone lost from thyroid removal. They do not affect antibody behaviour or prevent attacks on other glands.

options.text: Thyroxine tablets are needed only temporarily until the thyroid regrows
options.explanation: Once the thyroid is surgically removed, it does not regrow. Thyroxine replacement is typically lifelong.

options.text: The tablets cure the autoimmune condition that caused Graves' disease
options.explanation: Thyroxine tablets replace a missing hormone; they do not treat the autoimmune cause. The patient takes them because their thyroid was removed, not to address the antibodies.

toLevel5.stem: Compare the long-term prognosis for type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Which is likely to have a more predictable treatment course?

options.text: Type 1 has a more predictable course because the treatment is clear from diagnosis: lifelong insulin injections to replace what beta cells can no longer produce
options.explanation: Type 1 requires insulin from the start and throughout life. Type 2 is less predictable — it may initially be managed with lifestyle changes but progressively worsens as beta cells exhaust, with the timing of insulin need varying greatly between patients.

options.text: Type 2 is more predictable because all patients respond identically to diet and exercise
options.explanation: Type 2 progression varies greatly between individuals. Some manage for years with lifestyle changes while others need insulin relatively quickly. Genetic and metabolic factors influence the course.

options.text: Both types have identical treatment courses because both involve insulin
options.explanation: While both may eventually require insulin, the treatment journey differs significantly. Type 1 requires insulin immediately; type 2 starts with lifestyle management and progresses variably.

options.text: Neither type has a predictable course because both are autoimmune
options.explanation: Only type 1 is autoimmune. Type 2 involves insulin resistance and lifestyle factors. Type 1 has a more predictable course because the treatment (insulin replacement) is the same from diagnosis.

toLevel5.stem: Why do both diabetes and Graves' disease illustrate the importance of the normal hormone signalling pathway?

options.text: Because each condition disrupts a specific step in hormone signalling, and the resulting loss of homeostasis demonstrates how critical each step is for normal function
options.explanation: Type 1 shows what happens when hormone production fails. Type 2 shows what happens when target cells lose sensitivity. Graves' shows what happens when receptor binding is hijacked. Together they demonstrate every step matters.

options.text: Because both conditions can be cured by repairing the feedback loop
options.explanation: Neither can currently be cured. Diabetes is managed with insulin or lifestyle changes, and Graves' is managed by reducing thyroid output. The conditions illustrate pathway importance but cannot simply be 'repaired'.

options.text: Because both conditions only affect elderly patients
options.explanation: Type 1 diabetes often appears in childhood, and Graves' disease commonly affects middle-aged women. Neither is restricted to elderly patients.

options.text: Because both conditions involve the same hormone and the same gland
options.explanation: Diabetes involves insulin from the pancreas, while Graves' involves thyroxine from the thyroid. They affect different glands and hormones, but both illustrate disruption of normal hormone signalling.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher proposes developing a treatment that specifically targets the antibodies causing Graves' disease rather than the thyroid itself. Evaluate the potential advantage of this approach.

options.text: It could treat the root cause rather than the symptoms, potentially preserving normal thyroid function while eliminating the overstimulation
options.explanation: Current treatments reduce thyroid output (symptoms) but not antibody production (cause). Targeting the antibodies could stop overstimulation while leaving the thyroid intact and functional — a true treatment rather than management.

options.text: It would be unnecessary because current treatments already cure the disease
options.explanation: Current treatments manage symptoms but do not cure Graves' disease. Anti-thyroid drugs, radioiodine and surgery all target the thyroid rather than the autoimmune cause.

options.text: It would be dangerous because the immune system needs these antibodies
options.explanation: The TSH-mimicking antibodies are abnormal products of the autoimmune response. They are not needed by the immune system and their removal would be beneficial.

options.text: It would have no advantage because destroying the thyroid is always the best option
options.explanation: Destroying the thyroid creates lifelong hypothyroidism requiring daily medication. Targeting the antibodies could preserve thyroid function, which would be a significant advantage.

toLevel5.stem: Type 1 diabetes disrupts step {{blank:1}} of hormone signalling (secretion), while Graves' disease disrupts step {{blank:2}} (receptor binding) by having antibodies mimic TSH.
All three Graves' treatments target the {{blank:1}} rather than the {{blank:2}}, meaning they manage symptoms but do not cure the underlying disease.
